text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Health and Social Affairs Minister Margot Wallstrom says under no circumstances will the unregulated sale of alcoholic beverages be allowed in Sweden. An adviser at the European Court of Justice on Tuesday said European Union law was an "obstacle" to retail sales regimes for alcohol such as in Sweden where the state has a monopoly on alcohol sales.
- Housing built in Sweden between 1956 and 1973 during a campaign to build one million houses need to be examined for chemical substance PCB, an environmental group says.

- Transport prices between the Swedish island of Gotland and the mainland will increase now the government has decided to end a transport supplement. Vegetable and produce sellers on the island say this will adversely affect them.

- The Swedish state monopoly on retail sales on alcohol could be broken already this autumn. In a proposal to the European Court of Justics adviser Michael Elmer attacked the Swedish monopoly, saying it breaks European Union laws.

- Franco Modigliani, economist at Massachussetts Institute of Technology (MIT) in the U.S., thinks the German Bundesbank will succeed in keeping Germany outside Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU), he says in a column.

- Sweden's only aluminum smeltery Granges Metall, which is the country's most electricity intensive company, is worried about a new electricity production tax and more expensive electricity. Sweden's minority Social Democratic government has decided to start phasing out nuclear power in 1998, which produces relatively cheap electricity.
- Market players forecast the dollar will continue strengthening, reaching the eight crown to the dollar level. This would mean huge profits for export companies Volvo and Ericsson.

- More than half of European central bank employees, or 38,000 people, would become unneeded if a joint European central bank opened in 1999. There is a risk that Sweden's central bank would have to pay for some of their salaries.
- Many cabriolets are being shown at the Geneva car show in time for spring, including Saab Automobile's 900 Cabriolet and Volvo's new one.

- Carlsberg and Coca-Cola will set up a new holding company, Coca-Cola Nordic Beverages, to bottle and distribute beer and soft drinks in Denmark and Sweden. Norway and the Baltic countries may be included later.

- Investment company Industrivarden is suddenly hot -- the company's net asset value per share rose 50 percent to 501 crowns per share on February 28 from 333 crowns a share on January 1, 1996. The company posted a 20 percent fall in profits at 1.42 billion crowns after financial items for 1996.
